posts.text:
🇺🇸 Is AI finished after the Nasdaq wiped out its whole year? They said that about the internet in 2001 too

Sean Stone’s answer, on the day the Nasdaq dropped 5% and gave back all of 2026:

“I can’t imagine AI going bust.”

The filmmaker remembers the dot-com crash, when people decided there was only so much you could do online, right before shopping, video and friends on every continent showed up.

He wrote his new book with ChatGPT reading whole chapters and sending back notes in seconds, which is how he learned both what it’s good for and what it lacks.

When the chatbot tells him it laughed, Sean compares it to a sociopath copying feelings it has never had in a body.

Wall Street will eventually settle on a price for all this.

The harder job stays with the person typing, because a chatbot can hand over information all day and the thinking still can’t be outsourced.

@seanstonelives @WeTheBrandon

When a low-observable cruise missile flies at extremely low altitude at speeds over 800 km/h and remains in a neighboring country's airspace for mere minutes (in this case, about three minutes), requiring visual identification of the target before firing makes interception practically impossible.

The most effective way to protect Polish villages and airports (such as Rzeszów, where the air traffic control tower had to be evacuated for the first time) is not to wait for missiles to enter NATO territory, but to shoot them down on approach using allied air defenses or to provide Ukraine with more interception capabilities - we know what to do with them.

NIGERIANS, GO AND VERIFY (5) 

CONNECTING COMMUNITIES, UNLOCKING PROSPERITY: OUR ROAD INFRASTRUCTURE RECORD

Peter Obi

Another critical foundation of development is infrastructure, particularly road construction and maintenance.

Infrastructure is not just about constructing roads, bridges, and buildings. It is about connecting people, opening up economic opportunities, reducing poverty, and enhancing the well-being of ordinary citizens. A road that connects a farmer to a market, a patient to a hospital, a child to a school, or a manufacturer to a distribution centre is an investment in economic and human development.

This thinking informed our approach under the Anambra Integrated Development Strategy (ANIDS). We set out to connect all 177 communities in the State with motorable roads, paying particular attention to rural communities that had suffered years of neglect. Our objective was to build an interconnected road network that served the entire State, rather than concentrate projects in major cities or politically important locations.

I. The Road Revolution: Over 900 Kilometres of Road Projects

Between March 2006 and March 2014, during my two-term tenure in office, my administration asphalted over 900 kilometers of roads. These projects were deliberately distributed across the three senatorial zones of Anambra State to connect communities, facilitate commerce, and enhance transportation.

I acknowledge that Dr. Chris Ngige started the road revolution in Anambra State, and I commend the efforts his administration made in initiating several road projects. When we assumed office in 2006, we recognised the importance of continuing worthwhile projects rather than abandoning them simply because they had been initiated by a previous administration.

Among the roads we inherited from Ngige and completed were the Owerri–Ezukala–Umunze–Umuchu–Amesi–Uga–Igboukwu Road, where his administration stopped around Umuchu and we continued through Amesi, Uga, and onward to Igboukwu; the Iseke–Orsumoghu–Ukpor–Utu–Nnewi–Awka-Etiti Road, where his administration stopped at Ukpor and we continued towards Awka-Etiti; and the Ideani-Otuocha where work stopped around Awkuzu before our administration continued the project from Nteje to Otuocha.

There were also roads, such as Mmili John and Nkwelle Ezunaka bypass, which had been awarded before we took over, but on which no payment had been made by the time we assumed office. We took over these projects, assessed their status, and proceeded with the work. This was our approach to continuity in governance: acknowledging what had been started, distinguishing between projects merely awarded and those on which work and payment had actually commenced, and ensuring that important infrastructure projects were carried forward.

Some of the major roads and corridors included Amansea–Ebenebe Road; Aguleri–Umueze Anam–Mmiata Road; Nnewi–Ozubulu–Okija Road; and the Old Onitsha–Awka Road.

Other important projects included:

Awka and its Environs: Zik’s Avenue, Awka; Adazi-Nnukwu–Obeledu–Neni Road; 33 Junction–Nwafor Orizu College of Education Road; roads within the Awka Government Reserved Area (GRA); and the Old Nkpor–Amawbia Road.

Nnewi and Surrounding Communities: Nnobi–Nnewi Road; roads within Nnewi town; Akwaeze–Oraeri–Igboukwu Road; and Ekwulobia–Nkpologwu–Akpo–Achina–Umuchu Road.

Onitsha and its Environs: Bridge Head–Umunya Road; over 30 roads in other parts of Onitsha; more than 25 roads within the Onitsha GRA; over 20 stone-based roads within Harbour Industrial Estate, Onitsha; and the Nkwele Ezunaka Bypass.

Other Communities and Strategic Corridors: Awgbu–Amaokpala Road, with the Odor Bridge; Aguluezechukwu–Ogboji–Ajalli Road; Awkuzu–Igbariam Road, passing through the university; Owerri–Ezukala–Umuchukwu Road; Ugwuoba–Obosi Road; and Lilu Road.
